localChanges: All 17 `registerRules.ts` migrated and published, plus `core-game` and `civ1-game`. A clean reinstall resolves every one at its published version and the conformance checksums are unchanged — 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b, as they have been since before Stage 1.

`civ publish` now decides npm-versus-GitHub by `publishConfig.access` rather than by the installed path alone. A package `civ sync` placed is a plain directory with no codeload path to read, so path alone called `civ1-game` an npm package and offered it to `npm publish` — E402, because no `civ1-*` package is on npm. `publishConfig.access` is the right signal because npm already requires it: a new scoped package without it is restricted, so declaring it is exactly the act of opting in.

The gate also maps the `@civ-clone` scope onto the renderer's installed tree when compiling. These packages ship `.ts` beside their `.js` and TypeScript resolves the `.ts`, so a compile needs every transitive dependency's source — including one a package has only just declared. That is weaker evidence than a clean per-package install, and the conformance suite over the assembled tree is what covers the gap.

log: `core-data-object`'s `DataObject.ts` uses `BigInt` and `core-engine`'s `Engine.ts` calls `console.log`. Node resolution reaches those `.ts` sources rather than the compiled `.js`, so this package typechecks them — and under `lib: es2019` with no `@types/node` that is TS2583 and TS2584.
`npm run ts:compile` has therefore never succeeded here from a clean checkout. It only looked as though it did, because `tsc --build` skips when its outputs are newer than its inputs.

Stage 3 of the engine serialisation plan. `registerRules.ts` registered into the module-level `RuleRegistry` at import time, and each rule factory was called with no arguments so it picked up its own singleton registries. A second game in the same process would therefore share every registry with the first.

`register(game)` passes the game's registries to each factory instead. Which slot each parameter wants is not a judgement: the factories are already fully typed with the registry classes they take, so it is a lookup, and the codemod reads the signatures rather than guessing.

Importing the module still registers into `defaultGame`. The plugin loader works by importing each package for that side effect, and `defaultGame` adopts the existing singletons, so this changes nothing for anyone who has not moved yet. Dropping it would produce a game with silently absent rules — no error, just wrong behaviour.
The conformance suite's checksums are unchanged at turns 1, 10 and 50.

`core-game` holds the 43 registries every game has. `civ1-earth-generator` contributes two more, and they belong here rather than there: `core-` packages depend only on other `core-` packages, and baking one ruleset's registries into the shared context would break that as well as dragging a native `canvas` dependency in behind them.

`defaultGame` spreads `core-game`'s `defaultSlots` so the core registries stay the adopted singletons. Constructing the subclass with only its own slots silently gives it fresh ones, which would make it disagree with every unmigrated package about which registry is the city registry — a failure that shows up as a rule not firing rather than as an error. There is a test for it.

No `civ1-*` package is on npm — they are all consumed as `github:civ-clone/<name>`, so pushing the branch is the release. `publishConfig.access` implied otherwise and `private: false` is not a field the sibling packages carry.

Stage 3 of the engine serialisation plan, and the piece that unlocks the rest of it: multiplayer, test isolation, and loading a save into a fresh context rather than mutating the running game.

`Game` holds the 43 registries plus turn, year and the random number generator. The dependency injection it needs already existed — every class and every rule factory in the engine takes its registries as constructor parameters with singleton defaults. What was missing was something to pass.

`defaultGame` adopts the existing singletons instead of constructing its own. That is deliberate and it is what makes the migration incremental: while some packages still import `instance` and others take a `Game`, both must see the same registry. Otherwise a half-migrated engine disagrees with itself, and that failure looks like a rule not firing rather than like an error.
Two departures from the plan's sketch, both forced:

It sketched `core-city` re-exporting `defaultGame.cities` as its `instance`, which would make every registry package depend on `core-game` — a cycle. Adoption runs the dependency the other way and needs no change to the registry packages at all.

It also implied every registry in the tree. `civ1-earth-generator`'s two are excluded: baking a specific ruleset into core is wrong, and it would drag `canvas` in with it. What remains is 43, which is the count 01-constraints.md reached independently.

A ruleset's own context — `civ1-game` — subclasses `Game` and adds its registries. Constructing it with only its own slots silently gives it *fresh* core registries rather than the adopted singletons, so it would disagree with every unmigrated package about what the city registry is.
`defaultSlots` makes the fix obvious at the call site: `new Game({ ...defaultSlots, ...mine })`.

`Engine` carries the event stream a game runs on — `turn:start`, `player:turn-end` and the rest. Two games sharing one would each see the other's turns start, which makes it per-game state as much as any registry.

It is also the last parameter type the rule factories take that had no slot: across the seventeen packages with a `registerRules.ts`, 86 factories take 25 distinct parameter types, and with this one every single one maps to a `Game` slot. That is what makes the migration mechanical rather than a judgement per factory.
Three separate problems, all in the tests.

`expect(spy).called` and `expect(spy).not.called` are property accesses, not assertions — chai-spies wants `to.have.been.called()`. Every spy expectation in this file was a no-op, which is why 'should respect `Strategy` `Priority`s' registered two identical `Strategy`s, asserted a specific one ran, and never once failed.

'should filter inactive `Strategy`s' tested `canHandle`, removed in b1888be 'Remove `canHandle` from `Strategy` and `Routine`'. Nothing filters anything now. Its only live assertion was that `attempt()` returns true while a bare `Strategy` — whose `attempt` throws by design — was in the registry, so it passed or failed on which one the random tie-break put first: three runs in eight. Removed; 'should stop calling `Strategy`s after the first successful `attempt()`' covers the real behaviour.

The two remaining ordering tests now set an actual `Priority` `Rule` instead of relying on the tie-break, so what they claim to test is what decides whether they pass. Verified by inverting an assertion and watching it fail — worth doing after finding a file's worth that could not.

`"github": "civ-clone/civ1-diplomacy"` is a mangling of the entry directly above it, `"@civ-clone/civ1-diplomacy": "github:civ-clone/civ1-diplomacy"`, which is present and correct. As written it installs `github` from the registry — an unrelated, deprecated package, since renamed to `@octokit/rest` — on every install of this package.
